experiments.title: Does a Tree Give Water to the Air?
experiments.question: Do leaves give off water into the air? Is that one way a forest keeps itself damp?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you tie a clear plastic bag around a leafy branch in the sun, what will you see inside the bag after one hour? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, tie a second bag around a bare dry stick pushed into the same pot, in the same sunny place. Both bags stay on for the same time. Then only the leaves are different.
results_table: What I saw inside after 1 hour

materials.item: 2 clear plastic bags, clean and dry
2 pieces of string or rubber bands
a potted plant with plenty of leaves, such as tulsi, hibiscus or a money plant, in full sun on a balcony or by a sunny window, and a bare dry stick
a teaspoon or a dropper

experiments.safety: Choose a plant that is not thorny or poisonous, such as a hibiscus, guava or tulsi plant. Take the bag off after one hour. Leaves trapped in a bag in hot sun can get too hot and wilt.

schedule.what: Tie a bag around a leafy branch and one around a bare stick. Wait one hour. Collect and compare the water.

experiments.record: Draw both bags after one hour. Write how much water collected in each.
experiments.context: This is the tree water experiment. You tie a clear plastic bag around some leaves of a potted plant in the sun, and see whether the leaves give off water into the air.

setup.art: A clear plastic bag being slipped over a leafy hibiscus branch in sunshine.
setup.caption: 1. Slip a clear bag over a leafy stem of a potted plant in the sun.

setup.art: The bag tied at the stem with string, and a second bag tied over a bare dry stick next to it.
setup.caption: 2. Tie it tight. Tie a second bag over a bare stick in the same pot.

setup.art: After an hour, the bag on the leafy branch misty with drops collecting at the bottom; the bag on the stick still clear.
setup.caption: 3. After one hour, look and collect the drops.

flow.do: 1. Put the potted plant in full sun, on a balcony or by a sunny window. 2. Slip a clear plastic bag over a leafy stem, with plenty of leaves inside. 3. Tie the bag tightly around the stem. 4. Push a bare dry stick into the soil of the same pot and tie a second bag over it.
flow.say: We'll trap the air around these leaves. The second bag, over a bare stick, is our comparison. Only the leaves are different.
flow.kid: Put the plant in the sun. Put a clear bag over some leaves. Tie it tight. Push a bare stick into the pot and put another bag over it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the tree water experiment. You trap the air around some leaves in a clear bag.

flow.do: Leave both bags in the sun for one hour. Set a timer.
flow.say: Now we wait an hour. What do you think will happen in each bag?
flow.kid: Wait one hour. What will happen inside each bag? Guess.
flow.wait: Leave the bags for one hour, then come back.

flow.do: 1. Look at both bags before you touch them. 2. Take both bags off now, so the leaves do not get too hot. Hold the bottom corner of the leafy bag shut as you untie it. 3. Shake the drops into that corner. Open it over a spoon and let the water run in. 4. Do the same with the stick bag. 5. Write what you found.
flow.say: Look, the leafy bag is misty and has drops in it. Where did that water come from? We didn't pour any in. Let's take the bags off now, so the leaves do not get too hot.
flow.kid: Look at both bags. Which one has water inside? Take them off the plant. Collect the drops in a spoon.
flow.parent: On a warm, sunny day the leafy bag is usually misty within 15 to 30 minutes. After an hour there are usually many drops, sometimes a teaspoon or more. On a cool or cloudy day there may be only mist and a few drops: leave the bags on for two hours, or try again on a sunnier day. The bare-stick bag stays almost dry. This shows the water came out of the leaves. Plants pull water up from their roots and let it out through tiny holes in their leaves.

check.q: In the tree water experiment, the bag on the leafy branch got misty with drops of water. Where did the water come from?
options: From the leaves, which give off water into the air
From the rain
From the plastic bag
From the string
check.why: The bag was dry and closed, so the water came out of the leaves. Plants pull water up from the soil through their roots and let it out from tiny holes in their leaves. Picking 'from the rain' misses that the bag was closed and it did not rain. The bare-stick bag, which stayed dry, shows the plastic was not the cause.

flow.do: Talk about what this means for a whole forest. Then ask for what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Our one branch gave all these drops in one hour. A big tree has thousands of branches. A forest has millions of trees. All that water goes up into the air. That is one reason a forest stays damp, and it helps make clouds and rain. Now tell me: what do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: One branch gave all these drops. Think of a whole forest! Now say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: leaves give off water into the air. What I saw: the leafy bag had drops after an hour, the stick bag stayed dry. Why: plants pull water from the soil and let it out through their leaves. This is why a forest makes its habitat damp, and why cutting a forest can make a place drier.
flow.think: If a forest helps make its own rain, what might happen to the rain if the forest is cut down?

activities.title: Under the Stone

materials.item: a flat stone, a brick or a flowerpot that has been lying on soil for a while
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up lifts the stone, tilting it towards themselves, so anything underneath runs away from them. Do not touch centipedes or scorpions. Put the stone back gently.

schedule.what: Guess, lift a stone, count who lives under it, and notice how it feels.

activities.record: Draw what you saw under the stone. Write your guess and the real number of living things.
activities.context: If you have a garden or a park nearby: this is a short noticing activity. You lift a stone and look at the small world hiding under it. If you find nobody, that is a result too.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up crouching by a flat stone on garden soil, the child holding up fingers to guess.
setup.caption: 1. Guess how many living things are under the stone.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand tilting a stone towards themselves, revealing woodlice, an earthworm, ants and pale roots on dark damp soil.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up lifts it gently. Look quickly.

setup.art: The child touching the damp soil under the stone and then the dry soil next to it with the back of her hand.
setup.caption: 3. Feel the soil under the stone and next to it.

flow.do: 1. Find a stone, a brick or a pot that has been lying on soil for some days. 2. Ask your child to guess how many living things are under it.
flow.say: Before we lift it, guess. How many living things do you think are hiding under this stone?
flow.kid: Look at the stone. Do not lift it yet. How many living things are under it? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Under the Stone. You guess how many living things hide under a stone.

flow.do: 1. Lift the stone towards yourself. 2. Look quickly, because many animals will run. 3. Count everything you see: woodlice, ants, worms, beetles, centipedes, roots, white fungus threads.
flow.say: Quick, look! What do you notice? Let's count everything that is alive. What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to lift the stone. Look fast! Count every living thing. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: It's dark and wet under there.
Why are they all hiding here?
Where do they go when it rains?
There is nothing here. Maybe it is too dry.

flow.parent: Woodlice are small grey creatures with 14 legs. They are cousins of crabs and prawns, not insects. If you find nothing under the stone, that is a real result, not a failure. Write down 0 next to the guess. Then ask: why might nobody live under this stone? Is the soil dry? Is it in full sun? Was it moved recently? Try one more stone in a shadier, damper spot, or after rain. Even a bare stone is home to bacteria, too small to see.

flow.do: 1. Touch the soil under the stone with the back of your hand. 2. Touch the open soil next to it. 3. Put the stone back gently, the same way up.
flow.say: Feel the soil under the stone. Now feel the soil next to it. Which is cooler? Which is damper? Why do you think so many animals live under here, and not out there?
flow.kid: Feel under the stone. Then feel the soil next to it. Which is cooler and damper? Put the stone back gently.

check.q: Why do woodlice and worms live under a stone and not on the open ground next to it?
options: Under the stone is cooler, darker and damper
The stone is food for them
They are trapped and cannot get out
The open ground is too wet
check.why: Under a stone it is cooler, darker and damper. Woodlice and worms dry out quickly, so this small place gives them what they need. A place like this is called a microhabitat. Picking 'trapped' misses that they ran away when the stone was lifted, then crawled back under it. Picking 'too wet' is the opposite of what your hand felt.

flow.think: Is the space under the stone a whole world? Whose habitat is it?

activities.title: What Does the Crow Need?

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: If you go outside to watch, stay with a grown-up and keep away from street dogs and monkeys.

schedule.what: Choose one animal near home. Find where they get each of their needs.

activities.record: Draw your animal in the middle of a page. Draw six arrows to where they get food, water, air, shelter, space and warmth.
activities.context: In this activity, you choose one animal near your home, like a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel or a gecko. Then you find where they get each thing they need. Together, those places are their habitat.

setup.art: A child at a balcony pointing at a crow on a wire, with a notebook open.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one animal you can see near home.

setup.art: A child drawing arrows from a crow in the middle of a page to a dustbin, a water tank, a tree and the sky.
setup.caption: 2. Find where they get each of their six needs.

setup.art: A finished page with a crow in the middle and six labelled arrows: food, water, air, shelter, space, warmth.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your animal and their six needs.

flow.do: Go to a window, a balcony or the gate. Choose one animal you can see often, such as a crow, a pigeon, a squirrel or a gecko.
flow.say: Let's choose one animal we see every day. We will be detectives and find out what their habitat gives them.
flow.kid: Choose one animal you see every day. A crow? A squirrel? A gecko on the wall?
flow.context: This is the first step of What Does the Crow Need? You choose an animal near your home to study.

flow.do: 1. Watch your animal for a few minutes. 2. For each of the six needs, ask: where do they get this? 3. Write or draw each answer.
flow.say: Where does the crow find food? Water? Where do they sleep or nest? Where are they safe? Is there enough space for them? Where do they go when it is very hot?
flow.kid: Watch your animal. Where do they get food? Water? Shelter? Space? Where do they go when it's hot?
flow.parent: Good answers are places you can point to: 'the crow drinks from the leaking tap', 'they nest in the neem tree', 'they rest in shade on the water tank at noon'. If your child does not know, it is fine to say 'we don't know yet' and watch again tomorrow.

flow.do: Draw the animal in the middle of a page, with six arrows to the places you found.
flow.say: Let's draw it. All these places together are your animal's habitat. Their habitat isn't one spot. It is everywhere they get what they need.
flow.kid: Draw your animal in the middle. Draw six arrows to where they get each need. That is their habitat!

check.q: A crow drinks from a tap, eats from a dustbin, nests in a neem tree and flies over the whole street. What is their habitat?
options: Only the neem tree
Only the dustbin
All of these places together
The sky
check.why: A habitat is every place where a living thing gets what they need. For this crow, that is the tap, the dustbin, the tree and the street together. Picking 'only the neem tree' mixes up a habitat with a home or nest. The nest is just the shelter part of the habitat.

flow.think: If the neem tree were cut down, what would the crow have to do?

activities.title: Square Metre Safari

materials.item: 5 metres of string or wool
4 sticks or pencils to push into the ground
a measuring tape or a 1 metre ruler
a magnifying glass
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do this with a grown-up. Do not put hands into holes. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Mark out two squares, one in a lawn or open patch and one under a tree. Count the kinds of living things in each.

activities.record: Make a tally for each square: how many different kinds of living things you found. Then draw two bars.
activities.context: If you have a garden or a park nearby: This activity is how real scientists study habitats. You mark out a square, 1 metre on each side, and count every kind of living thing inside it. Then you compare two squares.

setup.art: Four sticks pushed into grass in a square, with string tied around them, and a measuring tape along one side showing 1 metre.
setup.caption: 1. Mark out a square, 1 metre on each side, with sticks and string.

setup.art: A child lying on her tummy at the edge of the square, looking through a magnifying glass at grass, ants and a tiny flower.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. Count every different kind of living thing.

setup.art: A second string square marked out under a tree, on fallen leaves.
setup.caption: 3. Mark a second square in a different place. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Push 4 sticks into the ground to make a square, 1 metre on each side. 2. Tie string around the sticks. 3. Do this in an open lawn or patch of grass.
flow.say: Scientists who study habitats often use a square like this. It is called a quadrat. We will count every different kind of living thing inside it.
flow.kid: Make a square with 4 sticks and string. Each side is 1 metre. Scientists call this a quadrat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Square Metre Safari. You mark out a square of ground to count the living things in it.

flow.do: 1. Look slowly at every part of the square, using the magnifying glass. 2. Count the different kinds of plants and animals, not how many of each. 3. Make a tally mark for each new kind.
flow.say: We're counting kinds, not numbers. Ten ants of the same kind count as one kind. A different ant counts as a new kind. Look at the soil, the grass and the tiny flowers.
flow.kid: Look closely at every part of the square. Make a tally for each new kind you find.
flow.parent: Children often find 5 to 15 kinds in a lawn: grasses, small weeds, ants, a spider, a beetle, a worm. Under a tree, with fallen leaves, there are usually more. You do not need names. 'Tiny brown jumping bug' is a fine name. If a square has very few kinds, that is a real result. Count the grass and tiny plants too, which are always there.

flow.do: Move the string square to a different place, such as under a tree, by a wall or near a tap. Count the kinds again.
flow.say: Now let's try a different place. Where do you think we will find more kinds of living things?
flow.kid: Move your square under a tree, or near a tap. Count the kinds again. Which has more?

check.q: In the Square Metre Safari, a lawn square had 6 kinds of living things. A square under a tree with fallen leaves had 14 kinds. Why might the tree square have more?
options: It gives more shade, damp, shelter and food from leaves
Trees scare animals away from lawns
We counted it later in the day
Squares under trees are bigger
check.why: Under a tree there is shade, damp soil, shelter under leaves and food from rotting leaves. More needs are met, for more kinds of living things. Picking 'counted later in the day' is a sensible worry. A fair test would count both squares at about the same time. Picking 'bigger' forgets that both squares were 1 metre on each side.

flow.do: Compare the two tallies. Draw two bars.
flow.say: Which square had more kinds? What did that place give that the other did not?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each square. Which had more kinds? Why do you think so?
flow.think: Scientists call the number of different kinds of living things biodiversity. Which places near your home do you think have the most?

activities.title: Nature Map of Our Walk

materials.item: a big sheet of paper
crayons or colour pencils
a small bag or box for fallen things

activities.safety: Collect only fallen things: leaves, feathers, seeds, twigs. Do not pick flowers or take anything alive. Wash your hands after the walk.

schedule.what: Walk, collect fallen things, note where each was found, and draw a nature map.

activities.record: Draw a map of your walk. Mark where each thing was found, and colour the map by habitat: shady, sunny, wet, dry.
activities.context: If you have a garden or a park nearby: you walk in a park or around your area, collect fallen things, and draw a map of where each one came from. A walk around your building works too.

setup.art: A child picking up a fallen feather near a tree, a small cloth bag in her other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Walk and collect fallen things. Remember where each one was.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a hand-drawn path, a tree, a tap and a grass patch, and small things glued next to each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a map of your walk. Put each thing where you found it.

setup.art: The same map coloured in green for shade, yellow for sun and blue for wet places.
setup.caption: 3. Colour each part: shady, sunny or wet.

flow.do: 1. Walk slowly in a park or around your building. 2. Pick up fallen things: leaves, feathers, seeds, snail shells. 3. For each, say out loud where you found it: at the tree base, in the grass, near water.
flow.say: Let's collect only fallen things. Each time we pick something up, let's say where we found it. Was it shady or sunny there? Wet or dry?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Pick up only fallen things. Say where you found each one. Shady or sunny? Wet or dry?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nature Map. You go on a walk and collect fallen things, remembering where each one came from.

flow.do: At home, draw the path of the walk on a big sheet. Mark the trees, the grass, any water. Put each thing on the map where it was found.
flow.say: Let's draw our walk. Here's the gate, here's the big tree, here's the tap. Where did the feather go? Where did the snail shell go?
flow.kid: Draw your walk. Put each thing where you found it.
flow.parent: Patterns often show up: snail shells and moss near water and shade, dry seeds and feathers in sunny open places. Point these out only if your child does not notice them first.

flow.do: Colour the map: green for shady places, yellow for sunny, blue for wet. Look for patterns.
flow.say: Look at the colours. Did different things come from shady places and sunny places? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Colour the shady parts green, sunny parts yellow, wet parts blue. What pattern do you see?

check.q: On a nature map, snail shells were found only near a leaking tap and in shady places. What does this suggest about snails?
options: Snails need damp, shady places
Snails like sunny paths
Snails are found everywhere equally
Snails live only in the sea
check.why: Snails dry out easily, so they live where it is damp and shady. The map shows that pattern. Picking 'everywhere equally' does not fit the map, which shows them in only some places. Some snails do live in the sea, but these were garden snails, found near a tap.

activities.title: Four Homes: Act and Move

materials.item: open space to move
4 sheets of paper with POND, FOREST, DESERT and SEA written on them

activities.safety: Clear the space of sharp corners and things that could break.

schedule.what: Move like the four habitats, then take turns acting out a meeting of the four habitats.

activities.record: Draw yourself as your favourite habitat, and write one thing it gives and one thing that is hard there.
activities.context: This is a movement and drama activity. You move like each of the four habitats, then take turns acting out a meeting where the habitats talk about what they give.

setup.art: Four paper signs on the floor in four corners of a room: pond, forest, desert and sea.
setup.caption: 1. Put the four habitat signs in four corners.

setup.art: A child swaying with arms up like tall forest trees; another child lying very still like a desert at noon.
setup.caption: 2. Move like each habitat when a grown-up calls its name.

setup.art: Four children sitting in a circle wearing paper signs saying pond, forest, desert and sea, talking.
setup.caption: 3. Act out a meeting of the four habitats.

flow.do: 1. Put the four signs in four corners. 2. Call out a habitat. Your child runs to that corner and moves like it. 3. The pond ripples, and the forest sways. The desert lies still at noon, then comes alive at night. The sea rolls in waves. 4. Call out a living thing too, like 'a frog in the pond', and your child moves like it.
flow.say: When I say a habitat, run to its corner and become it. Desert! Now it's noon, lie very still and hot. Now it's night. Who comes out? Sea! Roll like waves. Now dive down to the dark bottom.
flow.kid: When a grown-up calls a habitat, run to that corner. Become it! Desert at noon: lie still. Desert at night: come alive!
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Homes: Act and Move. You move like each of the four habitats.

flow.do: Take turns being each habitat: pond, forest, desert and sea. As each one, say what you give easily and what is hard in you. Then argue: who is the best home?
flow.say: I am the desert. I give lots of sunshine and space. But I have very little water. Who are you? What do you give? And who would want to live in you?
flow.kid: Be one habitat. Say what you give. Say what is hard in you. Who is the best home?
flow.parent: Let the argument go on. A good ending is when the children see there is no single best home: each one is best for some living things. If there are only two of you, each plays two habitats.

check.q: In the habitat meeting, which habitat is the best home?
options: The forest, because it has the most food
The sea, because it is the biggest
There is no single best one. Each habitat is best for the living things that fit it.
The pond, because it is the smallest
check.why: Each habitat gives some things easily and makes others hard. A camel does best in the desert, a fish in water. Picking forest or sea is a fine opinion, but think of the camel. The forest would be a poor home for them, and a camel would not manage in the sea.

flow.do: Lie down quietly for one minute. Imagine you are the deep sea floor: dark, cold and still. Then imagine a warm vent and its crowd of worms.
flow.say: Close your eyes. You are the deep sea floor. Dark. Cold. Still. Now, warm water seeps up through a crack. Feel the crowd of life arrive.
flow.kid: Lie still. Close your eyes. You are the dark sea floor. Now warm water seeps up. Life arrives!
flow.think: Which habitat did you feel most at home in? Why?

projects.title: Make a Habitat Corner: Water and Shelter for Wild Visitors

materials.item: a shallow clay bowl or a wide plate
a few stones to put in the bowl
an empty tin or a plastic bottle cut open, with no sharp edges
dry twigs, hollow stems, straw and dry leaves
string
a notebook for the visitor diary

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the tin or bottle and covers any sharp edges with tape. Keep the bowl shallow, with stones in it, so small birds and insects cannot drown. Change the water every day, so mosquitoes cannot breed in it. It takes one minute.

schedule.what: Choose a spot. Set up the water bowl. Build a small bug shelter. Start the visitor diary.
Watch for 5 minutes. Write any visitors.
Watch for 5 minutes. Write any visitors.
Watch for 10 minutes. Check the bug shelter gently. Count the week's visitors.
Watch for 5 minutes. Write any visitors.
Count all the visitors. Make a pictograph. Decide what to add or change.

projects.record: Keep a visitor diary: the date, the time, who came, and what they did (drank, bathed, rested, hid). On the last day, make a pictograph of all the visitors.
projects.context: This is a two-week project. You make a small habitat corner on a balcony, a window ledge or in a garden, with water and shelter, and keep a diary of the wild visitors who use it.

setup.art: A shallow clay bowl with three stones in it, full of water, on a balcony ledge in partial shade.
setup.caption: 1. Put a shallow bowl of water with stones in it in a shady spot.

setup.art: A cut tin packed tightly with hollow stems and twigs, tied with string to a railing.
setup.caption: 2. Make a bug shelter: a tin packed with hollow stems and twigs.

setup.art: A child's notebook page with a table of dates, times and little drawings of a bulbul, a bee and a butterfly.
setup.caption: 3. Watch every few days and write down the visitors.

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot: a balcony, a window ledge or a corner of the garden. 2. Pick a spot in partial shade, away from where cats can hide. 3. Ask: which of a habitat's needs will we give?
flow.say: We can't make a whole forest. But we can make a place that gives two needs: water and shelter. Then let's see who comes.
flow.kid: Choose a quiet, shady spot. We will give two needs: water and shelter. Who will come?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Habitat Corner project. You choose a spot to make a small habitat with water and shelter.

flow.do: 1. Put stones in the clay bowl. 2. Fill it with clean water, just to the top of the stones. 3. Place it in the chosen spot.
flow.say: Why the stones? So small birds can stand, and bees can land and drink without drowning.
flow.kid: Put stones in the bowl. Fill it with water. Put it in your spot.
flow.parent: In summer, a water bowl is often visited within a day or two by crows, bulbuls, mynas or sparrows. Bees and wasps land on the wet stones to drink. Remind your child to change the water every day.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up checks the tin or bottle has no sharp edges. 2. Pack it tightly with hollow stems, twigs, straw and dry leaves. 3. Tie it to a railing or wedge it somewhere dry, opening facing sideways.
flow.say: This is a bug shelter. The hollow stems are like tree hollows for tiny insects. Small bees and spiders may move in.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to check the tin. Pack it with hollow stems and twigs. Tie it up somewhere dry.

flow.do: Change the water every day, which takes one minute. On days 2, 4, 7 and 10, also watch quietly for 5 minutes (10 minutes on day 7) and write every visitor in the diary.
flow.say: Let's watch quietly. Who's here? What are they doing: drinking, bathing, resting or hiding?
flow.kid: Change the water. Watch quietly for 5 minutes. Write who came and what they did.
flow.wait: Change the water every day. Come back to watch on days 2, 4, 7 and 10.

flow.do: On day 14, count all the visitors in the diary. Make a pictograph: one small picture for each visit, in a row for each kind of visitor.
flow.say: Let's count. Who came most often? What did they use most: the water or the shelter?
flow.kid: Count all your visitors. Draw a little picture for each visit. Who came most?

check.q: In the Habitat Corner, birds and bees visited the water bowl often in summer. What does this show?
options: Water is a need that is hard to find in a town in summer
Birds only drink from clay bowls
Bees live in water
The bowl is their whole habitat
check.why: In a hot town, clean water is hard to find, so a bowl of water meets a real need. Picking 'their whole habitat' misses that they still need food, shelter and space elsewhere. Your corner gives only part of their habitat.

flow.do: Decide together what to add or change: a plant with flowers, more shade, a second bowl.
flow.say: If we wanted more visitors, which other need could we give? Food from flowers? More shade? Remember Jadav Payeng, from this unit's story: he made a place that gives, and life came.
flow.kid: What could you add? Flowers for food? More shade? Make your corner give more.
flow.think: Your corner gives water and shelter. What would it need to become a whole habitat for one bird?

challenges.title: Keep It Cool in the Desert
challenges.problem: Desert animals hide from the midday sun. Your job is to build a shelter that keeps a small cup of water as cool as possible in the hot sun for one hour. The cup of water is your 'desert animal'.
constraints: The shelter must fit in a shoebox.
Use only things from home, like cardboard, cloth, sand, leaves and paper.
The cup must be in direct sun, on a balcony or a sunny window ledge, not in the shade.
Measure the water's temperature at the start and after one hour.
materials: 2 small steel cups or glasses of water, filled from the same jug
a thermometer, if you have one. If not, dip a finger in each cup at the end and say which is cooler.
cardboard, cloth, newspaper, sand, soil, leaves, a shoebox
general: Make shade: put a roof over the cup, so sunlight cannot reach it.
Dig in: bury the cup partly in damp soil from a flowerpot, like a burrow. A little way down, the ground stays cooler.
Use a light colour: white cloth or paper on top reflects sunlight.
creative: Wrap the cup in a wet cloth. As the water evaporates, which means it dries off into the air, it takes heat away from the cup. A clay pot (a matka or kooja) keeps water cool the same way.
Make a thick roof with an air gap under it, like the thick mud walls of houses in the Thar.
Copy a termite mound: a tall chimney that lets hot air rise out.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shelter. Draw it, build it and test it against a cup with no shelter. Which kept your 'animal' coolest?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the desert habitat. Desert animals hide in burrows and shade by day. You build a shelter that keeps a cup of water cool in the hot sun.

setup.art: Two steel cups of water on a sunny step, one bare, one inside a cardboard shelter with a white cloth roof.
setup.caption: 1. Put one bare cup and one sheltered cup in the sun.

setup.art: A child pushing a thermometer into the water in each cup, with a timer set to one hour.
setup.caption: 2. Measure both cups at the start and after one hour.

setup.art: A notebook showing two temperatures, 42 degrees for the bare cup and 31 degrees for the sheltered cup.
setup.caption: 3. Compare. Which shelter kept the water coolest?

flow.do: 1. Fill two cups from the same jug. 2. Measure the temperature of both. 3. Put one bare cup in the sun. This is the comparison.
flow.say: This bare cup is a desert animal with nowhere to hide. Let's see how hot it gets. Then we'll design a shelter for the other one.
flow.kid: Fill two cups with water. Measure both. Put one bare cup in the sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep It Cool in the Desert. You set up a cup of water with no shelter, to compare with your shelter.

flow.do: List three ideas for a shelter before building anything. Then choose one.
flow.say: Think like a desert animal. Where would you hide at noon? Let's list three ideas first.
flow.kid: Think like a desert fox. Where would you hide at noon? Draw three ideas.

flow.do: 1. Build the shelter around the second cup. 2. Put it in the sun next to the bare cup. 3. Leave both for one hour.
flow.say: Build it, then put it right next to the bare cup, so both get the same sun. That keeps it fair.
flow.kid: Build your shelter. Put it next to the bare cup in the sun. Wait one hour.
flow.wait: Leave both cups in the sun for one hour.

flow.do: Measure both cups again. Compare. Then read the usual and creative solutions, and improve the design.
flow.say: How much hotter did the bare cup get? How much did your shelter help? What would a real desert animal do?
flow.kid: Measure both cups. Which is cooler? By how much? Now read the other ideas. Can you do better?
flow.parent: A shade roof usually helps a lot. Burying the cup in damp soil, or wrapping it in a wet cloth, often helps most. This is why many desert animals live in burrows, and why clay pots keep water cool.

check.q: In one made-up test of the desert shelter challenge, the bare cup reached 42 degrees and the sheltered cup only 31. What does this tell us about desert animals?
options: Shade and shelter make a huge difference in the desert
Desert animals like being hot
Water always gets hot in the sun, whatever you do
Shelters make things hotter
check.why: The shelter kept the water 11 degrees cooler. A desert gives sunshine and space, but very little shade. So shelter, like a burrow, is one of the most important needs there. Picking 'whatever you do' does not fit the results: the shelter worked.

challenges.title: A Balcony Habitat for Butterflies
challenges.problem: Butterflies need flowers to drink nectar from, plants for their caterpillars to eat, water and shelter from wind. They also need sun to warm their wings. Design a habitat for butterflies that fits on a balcony or a window ledge, about 1 metre long.
constraints: It must fit in a space about 1 metre long.
It must give at least four of a butterfly's needs.
It must use real plants that grow in your part of India.
No chemical sprays, which kill butterflies and caterpillars.
materials: paper, pencil and colours for the design
optional: pots, soil and seeds or cuttings to build it for real
general: Grow nectar flowers, such as marigold, ixora, zinnia or periwinkle.
Grow a host plant: a plant that caterpillars eat. Curry leaf and lemon plants feed lime butterfly caterpillars.
Put a shallow dish of damp sand for butterflies to sip from.
creative: Put a flat stone in the morning sun, for butterflies to warm their wings on.
Plant flowers that bloom at different times, so there is food all year, like a forest.
Join with neighbours, so many balconies make a long butterfly road through the city.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own balcony habitat. Label each part with the need it gives. If you can, build it and keep a diary of the butterflies that come.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design a small habitat for butterflies on a balcony or a window ledge, giving each of the things a butterfly needs.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a balcony railing with pots of marigold, curry leaf and lemon plants, a dish of damp sand and a flat stone.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your balcony space, about 1 metre long.

setup.art: The drawing with labels and arrows: nectar flowers for food, curry leaf for caterpillars, damp sand for water, stone for warmth.
setup.caption: 2. Label which need each part gives.

setup.art: Real pots on a balcony with a lime butterfly on a lemon plant.
setup.caption: 3. Build it if you can, and watch who comes.

flow.do: List a butterfly's needs together: nectar food, plants for caterpillars, water, shelter from wind, sun for warmth.
flow.say: A butterfly's habitat must give food for the butterfly and food for their caterpillars. They need different plants! What else do they need?
flow.kid: What does a butterfly need? Food for the butterfly. Food for their caterpillars. Water. Sun. Shelter.
flow.context: This is the first step of the butterfly balcony challenge. You list everything a butterfly needs from their habitat.

flow.do: Draw a design for a space about 1 metre long. Label each part with the need it gives.
flow.say: Draw your balcony. Where will the flowers go? The caterpillar plants? The water? Label each part with its need.
flow.kid: Draw your butterfly habitat. Label each part with the need it gives.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas together, and improve the design.
flow.say: Here are some ideas other people use, and some creative ones. Which would you add?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Add the best ones to your design.

check.q: A child's butterfly balcony has lots of marigold flowers, but no butterflies lay eggs there. What is missing?
options: Host plants for the caterpillars to eat
More marigolds
A bigger balcony
Nothing, butterflies never lay eggs on balconies
check.why: Many butterflies lay eggs only on the plants their caterpillars can eat. Lime butterflies need lemon or curry leaf plants. Flowers feed the adults, but not the young. Picking 'more marigolds' gives more of a need that is already met. A habitat must give every stage of life what it needs.

flow.do: Share the design with the family. If you can, build it for real.
flow.say: Tell the family what your design gives a butterfly. Could we build part of it?
flow.kid: Show your design to your family. Can you build part of it?
flow.think: If every balcony in your street had a butterfly corner, would that make a habitat?

items.p: Nila, a girl in Chennai, puts a bowl of water on her balcony. Next to it she hangs a tin packed with dry twigs. Which two needs of a habitat is she giving to small birds and insects?
items.why: The bowl gives water. The packed tin is a safe place to hide and rest, which is shelter. A strong answer also notices what is still missing: food, such as a plant with flowers. Picking 'food' forgets that water and twigs are not food.

items.p: A habitat gives a living thing food, water, air, space, the right warmth and a safe place to rest and hide. That safe place is called ____.
items.why: Shelter keeps a living thing away from sun, rain and hungry animals. A tree hollow is shelter for an owl. A crack in a wall is shelter for a gecko.

items.p: Sort these into the living parts and the non-living parts of a pond.
items.a: see items
items.why: Living parts grow, take in food and make more of their own kind. The green slime is tiny living algae, so it is living. Mud, water and sunlight are not alive, but every living part of the pond needs them.

items.p: At noon, the Thar Desert looks empty. So very few animals live there.
items.why: False. Many desert animals, like gerbils, foxes and beetles, hide in cool burrows in the heat of the day. They come out in the cool of the night. The desert only looks empty because we visit at the wrong time.

items.p: Choose one animal you can see from your window or balcony, such as a crow, a pigeon or a gecko. Where do they find food, water and shelter? Which of these was hardest to spot?
items.a: A strong answer names a real animal and a real place for each need, from watching, not guessing. For example: a pigeon eats grain that a neighbour throws down, drinks from a dripping AC pipe and sleeps on the ledge under the water tank. The hardest to spot was water, because I never saw them drinking until the second day.
items.why: A habitat is often more than one spot. An animal may eat in one place, drink in another and sleep in a third.

items.p: Olive ridley turtles spend most of their lives far out at sea. Yet each winter, thousands crawl onto beaches in Odisha at night. Why do they come ashore?
opts: To lay their eggs in warm, dry sand, which the sea cannot give
To find food on the beach
To rest, because swimming tires them
To get away from the cold sea
items.why: The sea gives a turtle food and space to swim. But turtle eggs must sit in sand to hatch, and only a beach gives that. So a turtle's habitat is two places: the open sea and one beach. A strong answer notices that one living thing can need different places at different times of life.

items.p: Match each living thing to the part of their body that suits their habitat.
pairs: wide, flat feet that do not sink in sand
big, waxy leaves that float and stay dry
a strong beak for picking fruit high in trees
flippers for swimming far in the sea
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each body suits the place where they live. If you swapped the habitats, the same body parts would be little help: flippers are slow on sand, and wide camel feet cannot swim.

items.p: A cactus lives well in a desert, but a cactus planted in a pond rots and dies. Explain why, using the word habitat.
items.a: A strong answer says that a cactus is built to store water and needs dry soil, so the desert is their habitat. In a pond, the roots sit in water all the time, cannot get air and rot. A pond is a good habitat for a lotus, but not for a cactus.
items.why: A habitat is good only for the living things whose needs it meets. Too much of something, like water, can be as bad as too little.

items.p: The damp, dark corner under a kitchen sink is a small habitat inside a bigger one. A small habitat like this is called a ____.
items.why: Micro means very small. Under a sink, under a flowerpot, a crack in a wall and the soil of a potted plant are all microhabitats. Each one can be cooler, damper or darker than the room around it.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? These are things that might help curd bacteria grow: milk, warmth, sunlight, time. Which do they not need, and why?
items.a: sunlight
items.why: The warm bowl in the three bowls test was wrapped in a towel, in the dark, and it still set first. So curd bacteria need food, water and warmth, but not sunlight. Plants need sunlight. Many living things do not.
items.context: Remember the three bowls experiment, where you stirred curd into warm milk and kept one bowl warm, one on the counter and one in the fridge?

items.p: A pond near Madurai dries up in April. What do some frogs do?
opts: Dig into the damp mud and wait there until the rain comes back
Stay on the dry cracked mud in the sun
items.why: Deep down, the mud stays damp and cool, so it shelters them until the rains fill the pond again. Picking 'hop to the sea' forgets that sea water is salty, and most frogs cannot live in it.

items.p: Draw a pond cut in half, so we can see inside. Show one living thing at the top of the water, one in the middle and one in the mud at the bottom.
items.a: For example: a lotus leaf or a water strider at the top, a fish in the middle, a snail or a worm in the mud. A strong drawing also shows where the light is brightest.
items.why: One pond holds several small habitats at different levels. The top gets the most light and air, and the mud is darkest.
items.art: An empty outline of a pond cut in half, showing the top, the middle and the muddy bottom.

items.p: A fish lives under water, so a fish does not need air.
items.why: False. Water holds a little air mixed into it, and fish take air in through their gills. That is why a fish tank has a pump that bubbles air into the water. Air is one of the needs of a habitat, even under water.

items.p: House sparrows used to nest in holes in old walls and under tiled roofs. Many Indian cities now have new buildings with smooth walls and glass. In many of these cities, sparrows have become rare. Which need of a habitat could be missing? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer names shelter: smooth new walls give no holes for a nest. It explains that a bird with food and water still cannot raise chicks without a safe nesting place. It may add one more possible cause, such as fewer insects to feed the chicks.
items.why: Scientists think the loss of nesting places is one reason, along with fewer insects for chicks. A habitat must meet every need. If one is missing, the living thing cannot stay, however much of the others there is.

items.p: A crow nests in a neem tree, eats scraps from the bins and drinks from the water tank on the roof. What is the crow's habitat?
opts: All three places together, and the space between them
The crow has no habitat in a city
items.why: A habitat is everywhere a living thing finds their needs. For this crow, that is the tree, the bins and the tank. Picking 'only the nest' mixes up a habitat with a home to sleep in.

items.p: Look at the chart from the five worlds test. An earthworm needs cool, damp soil. Which place would suit them best?
items.why: Under the leaves was the coolest place, at 28 degrees. Fallen leaves also keep the soil damp and give food as they rot. The sunny path was hottest and driest, so an earthworm would dry out there. A strong answer uses the numbers in the chart.
items.context: The five worlds test is an outdoor experiment: you measure five small places in one garden. Here are made-up results from it.

chart.title: Temperature in five places at midday

items.p: In the tree water test, why did we also tie a bag around a bare stick with no leaves?
opts: To check that the water came from the leaves, and not from the air or the plastic
To make the test take longer
items.why: The leafy bag filled with drops and the bare-stick bag stayed dry. So the water came from the leaves. Without the bare stick, someone could say that damp air made the drops. A strong answer calls the bare stick the comparison.
items.context: Remember the tree water test, where you tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun, and another around a bare stick?

items.p: Match each habitat with what is hard about living there.
pairs: it can dry up in summer
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: No habitat gives everything easily. Each one has its own problem, and the living things there have their own ways to handle it.

items.p: Ladakh gets very little rain and has freezing winters. What kind of habitat is it?
opts: It cannot be a desert, because it is cold
items.why: A desert is a place with very little rain, hot or cold. Ladakh is a cold desert. Many people think every desert is hot and sandy, but the word is about rain, not heat.

items.p: Sort these. Did people destroy a habitat, or protect or make one?
items: filling a pond to build houses
the women of Reni village guarding their trees in 1974
cutting a forest for a road
Jadav Payeng planting a forest on a sandbar
keeping a sacred grove uncut for hundreds of years
items.a: see items
items.why: People change habitats more than any other living thing. We can destroy them, but we can also protect them and even make new ones.

items.p: A gecko waits on the wall next to a tube light every night. What does that spot give her?
opts: Food, because insects fly to the light and she catches them
Nothing: she is there by chance
items.why: Many insects fly to lights at night, so the wall by the light is full of food for a gecko. That spot is part of her habitat. Picking 'by chance' does not fit, because she comes back to the same spot every night.
items.context: Geckos are the small lizards on house walls. They live in most Indian homes.

items.p: Before Jadav Payeng planted trees, snakes washed onto the bare sandbar died in the hot sun. Explain how the trees changed the non-living parts of the sandbar, so that animals could live there.
items.a: A strong answer names at least two non-living changes. The trees made shade, so the ground got cooler. Their fallen leaves rotted into soil. Their roots held the sand in floods, and the air under them stayed damper. Then animals found what they needed and came by themselves.
items.why: Living things change their habitats. Here the trees changed heat, soil and dampness, which are all non-living parts.
items.context: Jadav Payeng is a man in Assam who, from 1979, planted a forest on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra river.

items.p: People disagree about whether a zoo can be a good habitat for an elephant.

views.who: Lakshmi, who looks after elephants at a zoo in Mysuru
views.says: Here the elephants get food every day, clean water, shade and a vet. Nobody hunts them.

views.who: A scientist who studies wild elephants
views.says: Wild elephants walk many kilometres a day and live in big family herds. A zoo cannot give that much space.
Wild forests are being cut for farms and roads. Some elephants have nowhere safe left, so caring places are needed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason, using the six needs of a habitat. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the needs of a habitat as evidence. For example: space is a need, and a zoo cannot give enough of it. It then gives a fair point from another side, for example that food, water and a vet are needs too. It may say the best answer is to protect wild forests.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A zoo meets some needs very well and others poorly. The real argument is about which needs matter most, and what to do when wild habitats are lost.

items.p: Label the layers of a forest: canopy, middle layer, forest floor.
items.why: Each layer is a different habitat. Hornbills live in the canopy, where there is the most light and fruit. Climbers and small trees live in the middle. Frogs, worms and fungi live on the dark, damp floor.
items.art: A forest drawn in three layers with three empty label boxes.

items.p: In the mangroves of Pichavaram, in Tamil Nadu, the river meets the sea. At high tide the water is salty, and at low tide it is fresher. What is hard about living there?
opts: The saltiness and the water level keep changing every day
There is no water at all
items.why: Living things in mangroves must handle salt one hour and fresher water the next, and mud that floods and drains. Some mangrove trees push out extra salt through their leaves. Picking 'nothing is hard' forgets that every habitat has its own problem.

items.p: A habitat must be a big place, like a forest or a sea.
items.why: False. A habitat can be tiny: the bowl of warm milk was a habitat for curd bacteria, and the soil in a flowerpot is a habitat for ants and worms. What makes a place a habitat is that it meets the needs of the living things there.

items.p: A girl keeps her tulsi plant on a sunny balcony. Her cousin keeps the same kind of plant in a dark bathroom with no window. Predict which plant will do better after a month, and explain using the needs of a habitat.
items.a: A strong answer predicts that the balcony plant will grow better. It says that plants use sunlight to make their own food, so the dark bathroom does not meet that need. It may add that the bathroom plant will grow pale, thin stems that lean towards any light.
items.why: Light is part of a plant's habitat, because plants make their food from sunlight, air and water.

items.p: On a summer afternoon, the top of the sand in the Thar Desert can be hotter than 50 degrees. A little way down, the sand is much cooler. What does a burrow give a desert animal?
items.why: Sand is slow to let heat through, so a burrow stays cool in the day and warm at night. It is also a safe place to hide. Picking 'more heat' is the opposite of what the burrow does.

items.p: A forest helps make its own rain. Put these steps in order.
items: Tree roots take up water from the soil
Leaves give off water into the air
The damp air rises and forms clouds
Rain falls on the forest again
a: Tree roots take up water from the soil
Leaves give off water into the air
The damp air rises and forms clouds
Rain falls on the forest again
items.why: The bag test showed the second step: leaves give off water. Over a big forest like the Amazon, much of the rain is water that the forest's own leaves gave off. So the living trees change the non-living rain.

items.p: Some animals live in the forest canopy, and others on the forest floor below. Choose one need of a habitat other than light. Explain how the canopy and the floor give that need differently.
items.a: A strong answer picks one need and compares both layers. For example, water: the canopy is hot, windy and dries fast after rain, so canopy animals drink from rain caught in leaves and tree holes. The floor stays damp for days, which suits frogs, worms and fungi that dry out easily.
items.why: One forest holds several habitats on top of each other. The same need is met in different ways at each level.

items.p: In the five worlds test, the sunny path was 41 degrees and under the stone was 29 degrees. Farhan, a boy in Class 4, says: 'An earthworm would be fine on the path. It is only 12 degrees more.' What is wrong with his thinking?
opts: Earthworms breathe through damp skin, so the heat and dryness of the path can kill them
Nothing: 12 degrees is a small difference
items.why: For a small, damp-skinned animal, 12 degrees and dry ground are the difference between life and death. Remember the snakes on Jadav Payeng's bare sandbar. Farhan treats a small number as a small effect.
items.context: The five worlds test is an outdoor experiment: you measure five small places in one garden. Here are made-up results from it.

items.p: Two plant scientists argued for years about where one habitat ends and the next begins.

views.who: Frederic Clements, an American plant scientist, in 1916
views.says: The plants of a place live together as one team, like the parts of one body. Habitats have clear edges.

views.who: Henry Gleason, an American plant scientist, in 1926
views.says: Each kind of plant spreads out on their own, wherever their needs are met. Habitats blend into each other with no sharp edges.

items.ask: Which idea fits what you have seen, for example at the edge of a pond, or where a park meets a road? Give your evidence. Then say what the other idea gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses something real as evidence. For example: at the edge of a pond, the plants change slowly from water plants to grass, which fits Gleason. It also says what Clements gets right: from far away, a forest and a grassland look like two separate things with an edge.
items.why: Most scientists now side mostly with Gleason, because careful counts of plants along slopes showed each kind spreading out on their own. But maps still draw edges, because they are useful. Scientists still argue about how much plants depend on each other.

items.p: Tube worms live at deep sea vents. They have no mouth, and no sunlight reaches them. How do they get food?
opts: Bacteria living inside them make food from chemicals in the vent water
items.why: The bacteria use a chemical in the vent water to make food, and share it with the worm. Picking 'do not need food' forgets that every living thing needs energy. Before 1977, scientists thought all food chains started with sunlight.
items.context: Hydrothermal vents are cracks in the deep sea floor where water heated inside the rock comes out.

items.p: Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has an ocean of salty water under thick ice. No sunlight reaches it. Which discovery in the deep sea gives scientists hope that something could live there? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer names the deep sea vents found in 1977. It explains that life there gets energy from chemicals, not sunlight. So an ocean with no light might still be a habitat, if it has warmth and the right chemicals. It says honestly that nobody knows yet.
items.why: Every living thing we know needs liquid water and some source of energy. The vents showed that the energy does not have to be sunlight.
items.context: Hydrothermal vents are cracks in the deep sea floor where water heated inside the rock comes out.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether milk sets into curd faster with one spoon of curd or with three spoons. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would check.
items.a: A strong answer changes only the amount of curd: one bowl gets one spoon, the other gets three. It keeps the same milk, the same amount, the same kind of bowl and the same warm place. It checks both bowls by tilting them every 2 hours and writing down when each one sets.
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing, just as the three bowls test changed only the warmth.
items.context: Remember the three bowls experiment, where you stirred curd into warm milk and kept one bowl warm, one on the counter and one in the fridge?

items.p: In the Square Metre Safari, a lawn had 6 kinds of living things and a square under a tree had 14. Kavya, a girl in Class 4, says: 'Under trees there are always more kinds.' Is that a fair conclusion from one test?
opts: No. One test in one garden is a start, but we need to test more places
Yes, one test is always enough
items.why: One result can be a fluke. Scientists repeat tests in many places before saying 'always'. Picking 'tests cannot tell us anything' goes too far. The test is good evidence for this garden.
items.context: The Square Metre Safari is an outdoor activity: you mark out a 1 metre square and count the kinds of living things in it. Here are made-up results from it.

items.p: Some people say a city has no habitats, only buildings. Use three examples from your own home or street to argue against this.
items.a: A strong answer gives three real places and says who lives there and which need is met. For example: ants under the kitchen sink find water and crumbs, a gecko on the wall by the light finds insects, and pigeons on the window ledge find shelter from rain.
items.why: Cities are full of microhabitats. Wherever a living thing finds their needs, there is a habitat.

items.p: In the Square Metre Safari, we counted how many different ____ of living things were in the square, not how many of each.
items.why: Counting kinds tells us how many different living things a place can support. Ten ants of one kind count as one kind. A place with more kinds usually meets more different needs.
items.context: The Square Metre Safari is an outdoor activity: you mark out a 1 metre square and count the kinds of living things in it. Here are made-up results from it.

items.p: As curd bacteria grow in milk, they make the milk sour. That sourness stops many other germs from growing in it. Explain how the curd bacteria have changed their own habitat, and how that helps them.
items.a: A strong answer says the bacteria turned sweet milk into sour curd, so their habitat is now different from what they started in. Most other germs cannot grow in sour milk, so the curd bacteria have the food and space to themselves. It may add that this is why curd keeps longer than milk.
items.why: Living things change their habitats, and sometimes the change helps them. Trees make shade for their own seedlings in the same way.
items.context: Remember the three bowls experiment, where you stirred curd into warm milk and kept one bowl warm, one on the counter and one in the fridge?

items.p: Sort these. Is a living thing changing their habitat, or is the habitat changing a living thing?
cats: A living thing changes the habitat
The habitat changes a living thing
items: earthworms turn fallen leaves into soil
A living thing changes the habitat
a dry pond makes frogs dig into the mud
The habitat changes a living thing
trees make the ground below them shady and damp
A living thing changes the habitat
the cold of a fridge slows curd bacteria down
The habitat changes a living thing
corals build a reef that fish live in
A living thing changes the habitat
freezing winters make marmots in Ladakh sleep for months
The habitat changes a living thing
items.a: see items
items.why: It works both ways. A habitat shapes what its living things do, and living things change their habitat. The two depend on each other.

items.p: A grandmother says: 'All bacteria are dirty. We should kill every one of them with strong soap.' A grown-up's body has about as many bacteria living in and on them as human cells. What is the best answer to her?
opts: Most of those bacteria are harmless or helpful, and they help keep harmful germs out
She is right: all bacteria make us ill
Bacteria only live on dirty skin
Soap kills every bacterium on the body
items.why: Your body is a habitat for trillions of microbes. Most are harmless or helpful: tummy bacteria help digest food and leave less room for harmful germs. It is still right to wash hands before food, because a few kinds are harmful. A strong answer is kind and gives the evidence.

items.p: Put these habitats in order of size, from the smallest to the biggest.
items: the forests of the Western Ghats
a: the forests of the Western Ghats
items.why: Each one meets the needs of the living things in it, from curd bacteria to whales. Size is not what makes a place a habitat. The sea is the biggest of all, with life at every depth.

items.p: Scientists look for liquid water when they search for life on other worlds. Could life somewhere else live without water? Say what you think, and what evidence would change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer gives a view with a reason. For example: every living thing found so far, from vents to hot springs, needs liquid water, so I think life elsewhere will need it too. It then names evidence that would change the view, such as finding something living in a place with no liquid water at all.
items.why: This is an open question. Water is the best clue we have, but nobody knows yet whether life elsewhere must work like life on Earth.

items.p: When a forest is cut down, the animals can simply move to the next forest.
items.why: False. The next forest already has animals using its food, water and space, so there is not enough for newcomers. Many animals also cannot cross the farms and roads in between. This is why losing habitats is the biggest danger to wild living things.

items.p: Gaura Devi and the women of Reni hugged their trees in 1974 to stop them being cut. Explain how saving the trees also saved homes for other living things.
items.a: A strong answer says that the trees are habitats for birds, insects, monkeys and fungi, and that the trees keep the soil and the air damp. So cutting the trees would take away food, shelter and water for many others. Saving the trees kept the whole habitat.
items.why: When one big living thing goes, the habitat of many others goes with them. This is why losing habitats is the biggest danger to wild living things today.
items.context: In 1974, in Reni village in the Himalaya, Gaura Devi led the women of the village to stop men from cutting their forest. This was part of the Chipko movement.

quiz.p: Which sentence best says what a habitat is?
opts: The place where a living thing finds everything they need to live
quiz.why: A habitat gives food, water, air, shelter, space and the right warmth. A habitat can be big, like a forest, or tiny, like a bowl of milk. Picking 'any house' mixes up a habitat with a house. Picking 'only a forest' forgets ponds, deserts, the sea and tiny places.

quiz.p: A pet fish lives in a small glass bowl. She gets food, clean water and the right warmth. Which need of a habitat is she short of?
quiz.why: A tiny bowl gives very little room to swim. Space is one of the six needs, along with food, water, air, shelter and the right warmth. Picking food, water or warmth misses that the question says she has those.

quiz.p: Why can a camel manage in the Thar Desert, while a frog cannot?
opts: A camel can go many days without drinking, but a frog's skin dries out fast
The desert is too cold for frogs
quiz.why: A desert gets very little rain. A camel's body is built to save water, and a frog needs damp skin and water for eggs. Picking 'bigger' is not about the needs a habitat gives.

quiz.p: Where in a forest is there very little sunlight?
quiz.why: The canopy at the top catches most of the light, so the floor is dark and damp. Picking the canopy is the opposite: it gets the most light.

quiz.p: Why does the sea hold most of the living space on Earth?
opts: It covers about seven parts out of ten of the Earth, and life lives at every depth
Fish are bigger than land animals
quiz.why: The sea is wide and very deep, and living things are found from the bright top to the dark floor. Picking 'salty' or 'blue' describes the sea, but does not explain the space.

quiz.p: In the three bowls experiment, which bowl usually turns into curd by morning?
opts: The warm one, wrapped in a towel
None of them, curd only comes from a shop
quiz.why: Curd bacteria grow fast in warmth, so the warm bowl sets first. Picking 'the fridge' is a common guess, because curd is kept there. The fridge keeps curd from getting too sour, because the cold slows the bacteria down. Picking 'all three the same' misses that warmth was the one thing we changed.
quiz.context: Remember the three bowls experiment, where you stirred curd into warm milk and kept one bowl warm, one on the counter and one in the fridge?

quiz.p: In the three bowls experiment, the fridge bowl stayed runny. Then it was kept warm all day, and by evening it had set. What does this show?
opts: The bacteria stayed alive in the cold, and got busy again once the place suited them
Warm air turns milk into curd by itself, with no bacteria
The fridge bowl never had any curd in it
quiz.why: If the cold had killed the bacteria, the bowl would never have set. They slowed down in the cold and grew again in the warmth. Picking 'warm air by itself' is a good thought to test: a bowl of warm milk with no curd stays runny much longer.
quiz.context: Remember the three bowls experiment, where you stirred curd into warm milk and kept one bowl warm, one on the counter and one in the fridge?

quiz.p: A tree drops leaves that worms turn into soil. Which idea does this show?
opts: Living and non-living parts of a habitat change each other
quiz.why: The living tree and worms make the non-living soil, which feeds the tree again. Picking 'habitats never change' misses that living things change their habitats all the time.

quiz.p: In a flat, ants come to the corner by the kitchen sink, but hardly ever to a dry, clean bookshelf. Why?
opts: The sink corner gives them water and crumbs of food
quiz.why: A habitat is where a living thing finds what they need. The sink corner gives ants water and food, so it is part of their habitat. Picking 'by chance' does not fit, because they keep going to the same place. Ants climb walls easily, so height is not the reason.
quiz.context: Ants live in nearly every Indian home. This question is about where in a flat you see them.

quiz.p: In 2019, scientists who studied wild plants and animals all over the world named the biggest danger to them. What was it?
opts: Losing their habitats, as forests are cut and ponds are filled
quiz.why: Changing land and sea for human use is the main cause of the loss of wild species. When a habitat goes, the living things in it lose their food, water and shelter.

quiz.p: Jadav Payeng made a forest on a bare sandbar. How did the animals get there?
opts: They came by themselves once the place gave them what they needed
They were brought by a zoo
quiz.why: He made the place give shade, soil and food, and the animals came. Picking 'carried them all' is impossible for elephants, and the story says the sandbar was bare at first.
quiz.context: Jadav Payeng is a man in Assam who, from 1979, planted a forest on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra river.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists NOT know yet?
opts: Whether there is life on any other world
Whether fish live in the sea
Whether warmth helps milk with curd in it to set
quiz.why: Nobody knows yet if life lives anywhere except Earth. The others have been tested and are agreed.

quiz.p: What did scientists find in 1977 at warm vents more than two kilometres down in the sea?
opts: Crowds of worms, clams and crabs, living with no sunlight
quiz.why: They expected an empty, dark floor. They found life fed by bacteria that make food from chemicals. Picking 'nothing at all' is what they expected before they looked.

quiz.p: Why is your body a habitat?
opts: Trillions of microbes live in and on it, and it gives them food, water and warmth
Because you live in a house
quiz.why: Your body meets the needs of trillions of tiny living things, just as a pond meets the needs of a frog. Picking 'not a habitat' forgets the microbes in your tummy and on your skin.

applications: Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks protect whole habitats, not just single animals.
Farmers keep ponds, hedges and trees on their land so that frogs, birds and bees, which help crops, have homes.
City planners leave lakes, wetlands and tree belts so the city stays cooler and has fewer floods.
Gardeners grow host plants and nectar flowers to bring butterflies.
Scientists count living things in squares, called quadrats, to check whether a habitat is healthy.
Zoos and aquariums try to copy habitats, with water, shelter, warmth and space.
People who plant mangroves along coasts protect villages from storms and give fish a nursery.
Bird baths and water bowls on balconies help birds survive Indian summers.
Engineers studied termite mounds to design buildings that stay cool without much electricity.
Space scientists study life at deep sea vents and in very hot springs to know where to look for life on other worlds.
Doctors study the microbes in our bodies, our inner habitat, to help with digestion and illness.
Fisheries protect coral reefs and mangroves, because many fish grow up there.

open_questions.q: Is there life anywhere other than Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Mars, Europa and Enceladus may have liquid water, but nobody has yet found any living thing beyond Earth.

open_questions.q: What are the limits of where life can live?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding microbes in hotter, deeper, saltier and colder places than they thought possible. Nobody knows where the real limit is.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living things share Earth's habitats?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have named about two million kinds. Estimates of how many exist in total range from several million to far more, mostly tiny insects and microbes no one has named.

open_questions.q: How much life is hidden deep inside the Earth's rocks?
open_questions.why_open: Microbes have been found kilometres down in mines and boreholes. Some scientists think there may be a huge amount of life down there, but it is very hard to measure.

open_questions.q: Do habitats have real edges, or are they just names we give?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have argued about this since Clements and Gleason, about a hundred years ago. Both ideas are partly right, and the answer may depend on the place.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the microbes in our bodies affect our health and even our mood?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found many links, but which microbes do what, and why, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Can a destroyed habitat ever be fully brought back?
open_questions.why_open: Some forests and wetlands have been restored, but scientists argue about whether they ever become exactly what they were, and how long it takes.

maths.problem: In a made-up five worlds test, the sunny path was 41 degrees Celsius. Under the stone, it was 29 degrees Celsius. How many degrees cooler was it under the stone?
maths.explain: The path was 41 degrees. Under the stone was 29 degrees. 41 take away 29 is 12. You can check by counting on: 29 and 1 makes 30, and 11 more makes 41. 1 + 11 = 12.
maths.context: The five worlds test is an outdoor experiment: you measure five small places in one garden. Here are made-up results from it.

chart.title: Temperature on the path and under a stone

maths.why_maths: Saying 'cooler' is a start. Finding the difference tells us how much cooler, which is how we know a microhabitat really has its own weather.

maths.problem: In a made-up three bowls test, a family gently tilted the bowls to check them every 2 hours. The warm bowl had set at 6 hours. The counter bowl set at 10 hours. The fridge bowl was still runny at 24 hours. Where were the bacteria busiest? How many hours sooner did that bowl set than the counter bowl?
maths.answer: The warm bowl. It set 4 hours sooner than the counter bowl.
maths.explain: The bowl that sets first is where the bacteria grew fastest. That is the warm bowl, at 6 hours. The counter bowl took 10 hours. 10 take away 6 is 4. So the warm bowl set 4 hours sooner. The fridge bowl had not set even after 24 hours, so the bacteria were slowest there.
maths.context: This is about the three bowls experiment. You stirred curd into warm milk in three bowls and kept them warm, on the counter and in the fridge.
maths.why_maths: Counting the hours each bowl took turns 'sooner' and 'later' into numbers we can compare.

chart.title: Made-up example: hours until each bowl set
chart.note: The fridge bowl had not set at 24 hours, so its bar stops at 24.

maths.problem: In a made-up tree water test, one leafy branch gave 2 teaspoons of water in one hour. A small tree has 10 branches like this one. How much water might the whole tree give in one hour?
maths.explain: Each branch gave 2 teaspoons. There are 10 branches. 10 groups of 2 is 20. So the tree might give about 20 teaspoons in one hour. A big forest tree has many more branches, so they give much more.
maths.context: This is about the tree water test. You tied a clear bag around a leafy branch in the sun and collected the water that came out of the leaves.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lets us go from one branch to a whole tree, and then to imagine how much water a whole forest gives the air.

maths.problem: In a made-up Square Metre Safari, the lawn square had these kinds of living things: 2 kinds of grass, 2 kinds of small plants, 1 kind of ant and 1 kind of spider. The square under a tree had 14 kinds. How many more kinds were under the tree?
maths.explain: First add the lawn: 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 kinds. Then find the difference: 14 take away 6 is 8. So the square under the tree had 8 more kinds of living things.
maths.context: The Square Metre Safari is an outdoor activity: you mark out a 1 metre square and count the kinds of living things in it. Here are made-up results from it.

chart.title: Kinds of living things in two squares

maths.why_maths: Sorting finds into kinds and counting them is how scientists measure biodiversity, so they can compare habitats fairly.

maths.problem: In the Habitat Corner diary, these visits were seen at the water bowl in two weeks: crows 6, bulbuls 4, sparrows 3, bees 8. Make a pictograph where one picture stands for 2 visits. How many pictures does each row need?
maths.answer: Crows 3 pictures, bulbuls 2, sparrows 1 and a half, bees 4.
maths.explain: Each picture means 2 visits. Crows: 6 divided by 2 is 3. Bulbuls: 4 divided by 2 is 2. Sparrows: 3 is one 2 and one more, so 1 whole picture and a half picture. Bees: 8 divided by 2 is 4.
maths.context: This is about the Habitat Corner project. You put out a bowl of water and a bug shelter, and kept a diary of who visited for two weeks.

chart.title: Visits to the water bowl in two weeks

maths.why_maths: A pictograph shows at a glance who used the habitat corner most, so we can see which need it met best.
