roots.context: We found that warm milk can be a home for curd bacteria, and that a dark sea floor can be a home for giant worms. Now we ask what habitats tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Curd bacteria turned warm milk into curd by morning. In the fridge, the same milk and the same bacteria stayed milk. A place is a home only for living things whose needs it meets. So a place that seems empty to us may be full of life that needs other things.
deep_truth.habit: We learn habitats as a list of places on a map: pond, forest, desert, sea. So we think the place alone decides who lives there, and we judge every place by what we need. But the same bowl of milk was a home for bacteria in a warm corner and not in the fridge. And the dark sea floor that people called empty was crowded with life.
deep_truth.evidence: In the three bowls experiment, the same milk and the same curd set only where it was warm. In 1977, scientists found worms, clams and crabs living where no sunlight ever reaches, fed by bacteria that make food from chemicals.

three.who_am_i: You are a good match for some places: ones with air, water, food and the right warmth. And your warm, damp body is a perfect match for trillions of bacteria.
three.what_is_life: Living things sense their surroundings and look for places that suit them. Curd bacteria wait in the cold and get busy again when it is warm.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not empty places with a few homes in between. Almost every place is a home for someone, even if it is not a home for us.

roots.thread: Habitats show how much variety life has. Each kind of living thing needs something different, so life has found a way into almost every corner of the Earth: ponds, deserts, warm milk, your tummy and the dark sea floor. No single kind of life could fill the world alone. Together, the many kinds fill nearly every place there is.

teachings.teaching: Everything in this changing world is filled with the one Lord. So enjoy the world without grabbing it. Do not covet anyone's wealth.
teachings.link: A habitat is shared by everyone who lives in it. When one living thing takes too much, as people do when they cut a whole forest, everyone in that habitat loses.

teachings.teaching: The first lecture of this Jain text teaches that earth, water, fire, air and plants are living beings, as well as the creatures that move. It asks people to act with care, so as not to harm them.
teachings.link: Jain teachers saw life in places most people call empty. Their earth and water beings are not the same as bacteria. But much later, microscopes did show bacteria living in soil, water, air and milk.

teachings.source: Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949), 'The Land Ethic'
teachings.teaching: We should see ourselves not as conquerors of the land, but as plain members and citizens of the community of soil, water, plants and animals.
teachings.link: People are members of habitats, not owners of them. That is why habitat loss harms us too.

science.text: At deep sea vents, bacteria make food from chemicals in the warm vent water instead of from sunlight. Tube worms, clams and crabs live off them.
Bacteria send chemical signals to each other, and change what they do when enough of them are close together. Scientists call this quorum sensing. Some curd bacteria use such signals too.

other_view.view: In their view, bacteria grow faster in warmth simply because the chemistry inside them runs faster, the way sugar dissolves faster in hot water. They say words like 'wait', 'sense' and 'choose' are only a way of speaking about bacteria. They also say a habitat is a real place that can be studied on its own, whoever lives there.

practice.title: Who is this place a home for?
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Hold one hand near your tummy, without touching. Feel how warm you are. Your warm, damp body is a home for trillions of bacteria right now. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out. Now open your eyes and look around the room. Pick one spot, like a corner, a windowsill or a flowerpot. Ask quietly: who might this place be a home for?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hold a hand near your tummy. Feel how warm you are. Tiny bacteria live there. Open your eyes. Pick one spot. Who might live there?

ask: People once thought the dark deep sea floor had almost no life. Why do you think they were so sure?
Is any place on Earth truly empty, or only empty of things like us?
The fridge was a poor home for curd bacteria, but a good place to keep curd. Who decides whether a place is good?
If trillions of bacteria live in you, are they part of you, or are you their home?
roots.art: A child at a kitchen table with three bowls of milk and curd, and around the edges small windows into other homes: a frog in a pond, tube worms by a deep sea vent, a camel in sand, and tiny bacteria in a bowl.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, scientists believed that every living thing on Earth depended on sunlight. Plants catch light and make food, and every animal eats plants, or eats animals that ate plants. So the deep sea floor, where no light ever reaches, was thought to have only a little life, living on scraps that sink from above. In 1976, Kathleen Crane, a young student scientist, towed an instrument she had helped build just above the sea floor near the Galapagos Islands. It found spots where the water was slightly warmer. In February 1977, she guided the next expedition back to those spots. The pilot Jack Donnelly and the scientists Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel dived there in the small submarine Alvin. Around cracks seeping warm water, they found giant tube worms, big clams and crabs. Holger Jannasch and other scientists then showed that bacteria there make food from a chemical in the vent water, hydrogen sulphide, instead of from sunlight. In 1981, Colleen Cavanaugh, a student, showed that the tube worms carry these bacteria inside their bodies. A whole habitat was running on the Earth's own heat and chemicals.
how_we_found_out.who: Kathleen Crane; the pilot Jack Donnelly with Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel in the submarine Alvin; Holger Jannasch; Colleen Cavanaugh
how_we_found_out.when: 1976 (Crane's warm-water survey); 1977 (the first dives at the Galapagos vents); 1981 (Cavanaugh's tube worm finding)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: All life on Earth depends on sunlight, so the dark deep sea floor must have very little life. The vent crowds showed that a whole habitat can run on chemicals from inside the Earth instead.

playtest: The core path works in a city flat. The three bowls experiment (e4) needs only milk, curd, three bowls and a towel. Milk that feels just warm on the wrist sets in the warm bowl overnight. The fridge bowl stays runny, and sets once it is moved somewhere warm. The counter bowl depends on the season: it often sets in summer and stays thick or runny in winter, which is a good thing to talk about. If no bowl sets, the milk was too hot or the curd too old: try again. The tree water experiment (e3) uses a potted plant in a sunny window or balcony, and gives fewer drops on a cool or cloudy day. Under the Stone, Five Worlds, Square Metre Safari, the Nature Map and Nature Bingo are extras for families with a garden or a park, and each says what to do if nothing is found.
